# Provide audio feedback when changing volume settings

## Headline

When the player adjusts the SFX volume slider in SettingsScene, a brief audible blip plays — its pitch rises with higher volume and falls with lower volume — so the player always knows the current level.

## Problem statement

The volume slider currently gives no audible indication of the selected volume. In a game where visual attention may be elsewhere and audio is the primary feedback channel, players need to hear the current volume level when they change it.

## Users

- **Player** (primary): adjusts volume during gameplay via pause menu or from the main menu.
- **Player** (secondary, during setup): sets volume for the first time without knowing what level is "loud enough" or "too quiet".

**User story:** *As a player, I want to hear a sound that indicates the current SFX volume level every time I change it, so that I can confirm the setting without guessing.*

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1 — Volume-change tone on keyboard input:** When the volume slider is focused and the player presses Left/Right arrow (or mapped keys), a short blip tone plays after each nudge (±0.05). The tone's frequency scales linearly from 220 Hz (at volume 0.00) to 880 Hz (at volume 1.00).
- **AC2 — Volume-change tone on pointer drag release:** When the player clicks and drags the slider and releases, a single blip tone plays corresponding to the new volume value. No tone plays during the drag — only on release (pointerup).
- **AC3 — Tone character:** The feedback is a single short (≤ 60 ms) sine blip with a smooth gain envelope (exponential decay to silence). It routes through the existing master SFX gain node so it respects the current mute state and volume.
- **AC4 — Safe degradation:** If no AudioContext is available (headless tests, autoplay-blocked), the function is a safe no-op — no errors, no thrown exceptions.
- **AC5 — Tests:** Unit/integration tests verify: tone frequency maps to volume on keyboard nudge, single tone on drag release (no intermediate tones), tone respects mute state (silenced when muted), and safe no-op without AudioContext.

## Constraints

- Must use existing `blip()` synthesis helper in `effects.ts` — no new audio assets.
- Tone volume must be low (≤ 0.08) to avoid being jarring compared to gameplay SFX.
- No new module files — integrate into existing SettingsScene.

## Existing state

- `SettingsScene.ts` implements a 0.0–1.0 SFX volume slider with keyboard (ArrowLeft/Right, step 0.05) and pointer drag interaction.
- `effects.ts` provides `setSfxVolume()`, `setSfxMuted()`, and the `blip()` synthesis helper used throughout the game for audio cues.
- The master SFX gain node routes all SFX through it; `setSfxMuted` zeroes the gain.
- Settings are persisted via `ai_hell_settings` localStorage key.

## Desired change

Add a `playVolumeFeedback(volume: number)` helper in `effects.ts` (or inline in SettingsScene) that plays a volume-mapped blip on every volume change. Call it from:
- `setVolume()` after the value is applied (for keyboard nudges)
- The `pointerup` handler on the slider track (for drag release)

## Key Files (predicted)

- `src/audio/effects.ts` — Add `playVolumeFeedback(volume: number): void` helper
- `src/audio/effects.test.ts` — Tests for `playVolumeFeedback`
- `src/scenes/SettingsScene.ts` — Wire feedback calls into `setVolume()` and slider drag release
- `src/scenes/SettingsScene.test.ts` — Tests for volume feedback integration

## Related work

- **AH-0MUA8BEUR006RWCI** (SettingsScene: SFX volume slider + mute toggle) — parent work item that built the slider; this adds feedback on top.
- **AH-0MUA8B6MT006M1KS** (SFX master volume + mute plumbing) — the master gain plumbing that volume feedback routes through.
- **AH-0MU9LPZ0G0015292** (In-game menu) — the broader menu system.

## Risks and assumptions

- **Assumption — tone mapping:** A linear pitch mapping from volume (220–880 Hz) provides clear, perceptually distinct feedback across the full range. Alternative mappings (logarithmic, exponential) are possible but linear is simplest and matches existing audio conventions in the codebase.
- **Risk — tone during drag could be jarring.** Mitigation: only play tone on drag *release*, never during the drag. This is a deliberate design choice; if the producer prefers live feedback during drag, that is a scope expansion.
- **Risk — tone might be inaudible when muted.** Mitigation: this is correct behaviour; the tone itself is volume feedback, and when muted the player cannot hear any SFX anyway. An audible "muted" click on the mute toggle is out of scope (see clarification below).
- **Risk — tone timing conflicts with gameplay audio.** Mitigation: the tone is ≤ 60 ms and low volume; existing cues (shoot, destruction) are similarly short. No conflict expected.
- **Scope — mute toggle feedback:** Toggling mute should NOT produce feedback in this work item. A "muted" click cue is a separate enhancement.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q: **What kind of audio feedback should indicate the volume level?** — Answer (engineer@Map): A short blip whose pitch scales linearly with volume — 220 Hz at 0.00, 880 Hz at 1.00. Rationale: follows the existing `blip()` synthesis pattern used throughout the codebase for audio cues; provides clearly perceptible pitch difference across the range. Source: codebase review of `effects.ts`.
- Q: **Should feedback play on every change (including during a drag), or only when the drag is released?** — Answer (engineer@Map): Only on drag release and after each keyboard step. Playing during a drag would produce rapid overlapping tones that are jarring and unhelpful. Source: UX best practice + codebase slider pattern (`_sliderFromPointer` called per-move, `pointerup` fires on release).
- Q: **Should toggling mute also produce feedback?** — Answer (engineer@Map): Out of scope for this work item. A mute-toggle audio cue is a separate enhancement. Source: scope isolation — this work item is about *volume* feedback specifically.

## Plan review notes (plan skill — 2026-09-27)

Plan decision: **auto-complete** (effort Extra Small, risk Low → below the planning threshold). The six automated review stages ran against the existing content; no child items were created.

### Integration precision (AC2 — no tone during drag)

The **Desired change** sketch specifies calling `playVolumeFeedback()` from `setVolume()`. `setVolume()` is also invoked on every pointer move while dragging (`_sliderFromPointer` → `setVolume`), so that sketch would emit a tone on every drag step and contradict **AC2** ("No tone plays during the drag — only on release"). The AC-preserving resolution (intent unchanged) is:

- Keyboard path: call `playVolumeFeedback(this.sfxVolume)` from `_nudgeVolume()` (reached only via ArrowLeft/ArrowRight while the slider is focused), not from `setVolume()` itself.
- Drag path: in the scene-level `pointerup` handler, capture `const wasDragging = this.dragging` **before** `this.dragging = false`, and call `playVolumeFeedback(this.sfxVolume)` only when `wasDragging` was `true`. A pointer-up that did not follow a slider drag must not emit a tone.

### Appendix (continued)

- **OPEN QUESTION** (producer): The plan sketch names `setVolume()` as the keyboard-nudge hook, which conflicts with **AC2** because `setVolume()` also runs per pointer-move. The plan skill has recorded the AC-preserving interpretation above (keyboard path + single tone on real drag release) and will not change AC intent without confirmation. Does the producer prefer **(a) AC-preserving: tone only on keyboard nudge and drag release [Recommended]**, or **(b) live tone during the drag (scope expansion; would require revisiting AC2)**? Directed to the producer because it shapes the audible UX; non-blocking under interpretation (a).
data.title: Provide feedback when changing volume settings

Refactor weapon fire rates as beat subdivisions and add catalogue-wide on-grid invariant

## Summary
Replace the hard-coded fire-rate constants in `src/utils/weapons.ts` with values derived from the 80 BPM beat period. Each weapon fires at an exact subdivision: cannon 2/beat (375 ms), spread 1/beat (750 ms), dual 1/beat (750 ms), rapid 6/beat (125 ms). Add a catalogue-wide test asserting every fire rate divides evenly into the beat period.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] **AC1** — All `WEAPON_*_FIRE_RATE` constants in `src/utils/weapons.ts` become derived from the beat period (e.g. `beatPeriodMs / subdivisions`), not hard-coded literals.
- [ ] **AC2** — `WEAPON_CATALOGUE` fire rates match the producer-specified values: cannon 375 ms (2/beat), spread 750 ms (1/beat), dual 750 ms (1/beat), rapid 125 ms (6/beat).
- [ ] **AC3** — A catalogue-wide invariant test asserts `beatPeriodMs % fireRateMs === 0` for every weapon in `WEAPON_CATALOGUE`.
- [ ] **AC4** — Existing weapon tests still pass after the refactor (no behaviour change beyond timing).
- [ ] **AC5** — New weapons added to the catalogue must satisfy the invariant; the test fails if they do not.
- [ ] **Traces to parent AC3** — [ ] **AC3 — Per-weapon subdivisions + catalogue-wide invariant.** Each weapon's fire interval is an exact subdivision of the beat: **cannon 375 ms (160 BPM, 2/beat)**, **spread 750 ms (80 BPM, 1/beat)**, **dual 750 ms (80 BPM, 1/beat)**, **rapid 125 ms (480 BPM, 6/beat)**. A catalogue-wide test asserts every `WeaponDefinition.fireRateMs` satisfies `beatPeriodMs % fireRateMs === 0` (equivalently `fireRateMs × n === beatPeriodMs` for a positive integer `n`), so the future 20 BPM quarter-time weapon and any other new weapon are on-grid by construction.

## Key Files
- `src/utils/weapons.ts` — fire rates derived from beat period.
- `src/utils/weapons.test.ts` — invariant test.

## Risks
- Low: existing tests will verify no unintended behaviour changes. The rapid weapon (125 ms) is unchanged; cannon, spread, and dual rates change slightly.
data.title: Refactor weapon fire rates as beat subdivisions and add catalogue-wide invariant

Wire the shared beat clock into CombatScene and GymWeapons auto-fire

## Summary
Wire the shared beat clock into `CombatScene._autoFire` and `GymWeapons._autoFire` so the scene supplies and uses the same clock. The beat clock is anchored at scene/player start and advances with game time (pauses with the game).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] **AC1** — `CombatScene._autoFire` uses the shared beat clock; player shots are emitted on beat ticks.
- [ ] **AC2** — `GymWeapons._autoFire` uses the same shared beat clock.
- [ ] **AC3** — The beat clock is anchored at scene start and advances with game time.
- [ ] **AC4** — If the game pauses, the beat clock pauses with it.
- [ ] **AC5** — No per-scene duplicate beat modules — one shared instance.
- [ ] **Traces to parent AC2** — [ ] **AC2 — All player fire is globally quantised.** Player auto-fire (`Player.tryFire` and its callers in `CombatScene`/`GymWeapons`) emits shots only on ticks of the shared beat clock, phase-locked to the scene/beat anchor — never off-grid — regardless of when a weapon is collected or the frame rate. All simultaneously active weapons fire on the same shared grid (no independent, drifting cooldowns). Tests assert every emitted shot time is an exact grid tick.

## Key Files
- `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.ts` — `_autoFire` drives/uses the shared beat clock.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymWeapons.ts` — `_autoFire` drives/uses the shared beat clock.
- `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.test.ts` — beat clock wired into auto-fire.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymWeapons.test.ts` — beat clock wired into gym auto-fire.

## Risks
- Low: straightforward wiring. Must ensure the beat clock is instantiated once and shared.
data.title: Wire the shared beat clock into CombatScene and GymWeapons auto-fire

Make BPM and per-weapon subdivisions configurable via existing config plumbing

## Summary
Make the default BPM, per-weapon subdivisions (or fire-rate multiples), and quantisation behaviour configurable through the projects existing config plumbing (`src/core/rules.ts` and/or `src/core/constants.ts`). Include sane defaults. Tests must assert a config override changes the firing cadence.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] **AC1** — BPM is configurable through the existing rules/config system with a default of 80.
- [ ] **AC2** — Per-weapon subdivisions (or fire rates) are configurable through the same system.
- [ ] **AC3** — Config overrides are tested: changing BPM or a subdivision changes the firing cadence.
- [ ] **AC4** — No scattered hard-coded beat/rate literals — all values come from the config or are derived from it.
- [ ] **AC5** — The config system handles corrupt/missing config gracefully, falling back to defaults.
- [ ] **AC6** — Subdivisions are configured as positive integers and each fire rate is derived from the beat period, so the catalogue-wide on-grid invariant (parent AC3) holds by construction; a test asserts the invariant under a non-default config.
- [ ] **Traces to parent AC4** — [ ] **AC4 — All values configurable.** BPM, the per-weapon subdivisions/fire rates, and the quantisation behaviour are configurable through the project's existing config plumbing (`src/core/rules.ts` and/or `src/core/config.ts`/`constants.ts`; persisted where the existing pattern persists), with sane defaults — no scattered hard-coded beat/rate literals. Tests assert a config override changes the firing cadence.

## Key Files
- `src/core/rules.ts` or `src/core/constants.ts` — configurable BPM + subdivisions.
- `src/utils/beat.ts` — reads config for BPM.
- Tests for config override → cadence change.

## Risks
- Medium: choosing the right config home (rules.ts vs constants.ts). The ACs require at least one tested override path.

# Per-wave generation modes: curve-fixed, hand-authored fixed and dynamic runtime regeneration

## Goal

As a **designer**, I want to mark each configured wave with a **generation mode**, so one campaign can mix hand-authored set-pieces with curve-driven and runtime-regenerated waves.

Three modes (the default is (a)):

- **(a) `curve` — curve-generated, fixed at runtime.** The sequencer builds the wave from its `targetDifficulty` once; the composition is then fixed for the whole run. It only changes when the designer explicitly asks for a level/wave regeneration (the `Regenerate` action).
- **(b) `fixed` — hand-authored, never regenerated.** The wave composition is authored and used verbatim at design and runtime. It is never passed through the sequencer. Its difficulty is *derived* from its settings (shown read-only in the editor — see sibling item 2).
- **(c) `dynamic` — regenerated at runtime.** The wave is rebuilt from its curve by the sequencer at runtime, seeded from the run's RNG, so successive runs differ while remaining reproducible for a given seed.

## Context / existing state

- `DifficultyCurveRow` — `src/core/configTypes.ts:88` — currently `level`, `levelName`, `wave`, `targetDifficulty`.
- Codec/validation — `src/core/csv.ts:405` (`DIFFICULTY_CURVE_COLUMN_ORDER`, `parseDifficultyCurves`, `serializeDifficultyCurves`, `validateDifficultyCurveRow`) and the Vite dev writer `vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.ts`.
- Seeded config — `src/data/difficulty-curves.csv`.
- Builder — `src/waves/sequencedLevels.ts` (`buildSequencedLevels`), currently pure/deterministic and always curve-generated.
- Runtime wiring — `resolveCampaignLevels`/`PlayScene.create` (`src/scenes/PlayScene.ts:202,405`) and `WaveManager.setLevels` (`src/waves/WaveManager.ts:103`).
- Editor preview — `src/scenes/gym/GymCurveSequencer.ts`.

## Relationships

- **Supersedes / generalises Support mixed generated and scripted levels in a campaign (AH-0MUH7Q6HN0006QPD)** to per-wave granularity and adds the `dynamic` mode. Reconcile at intake: preferred outcome is that this item absorbs that scope and AH-0MUH7Q6HN0006QPD is closed as superseded or reduced to any residual per-level behaviour.
- Enables the sibling UI item (generation-mode control in the curve generator) and the default-on item.

## Desired behaviour

- Add a `generation` column (`curve` | `fixed` | `dynamic`) to `DifficultyCurveRow`, the codec (`DIFFICULTY_CURVE_COLUMN_ORDER`, parse/serialize/validate), the Vite plugin whitelist and the seed CSV. An **absent** value means `curve`, so existing 4-column files and `defaultDifficultyCurves()` keep working unchanged.
- The builder honours the mode per wave:
  - `curve`: unchanged — one sequencer call per level, composition fixed for the run.
  - `fixed`: use the hand-authored composition verbatim; **never** call the sequencer for that wave.
  - `dynamic`: call the sequencer at wave-build time using an injectable run seed/RNG so the wave differs between runs but is reproducible for a given seed.
- Determinism contract: `curve` and `fixed` waves are independent of the seed; `dynamic` waves are a pure function of (curve, candidate pool, seed).
- Fallback: missing/unknown mode ⇒ `curve`; a malformed mode is treated like any other malformed row (dropped, existing file-level default-curve fallback preserved). A `fixed` wave whose composition cannot be resolved must fall back safely, never crash the run.
- **Open decision (resolve at intake):** where a `fixed` wave's composition is stored. Preferred: reuse the hand-authored static `LEVELS` wave for the same level/wave number. Alternative: persist an explicit serialized composition (groups) in the campaign config. Document whichever is chosen, including behaviour for levels numbered beyond `LEVEL_COUNT`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The generation-mode column round-trips: `parseDifficultyCurves(serializeDifficultyCurves(rows))` preserves each wave's mode.
- Absent mode defaults to `curve`; existing 4-column CSV rows and `defaultDifficultyCurves()` output are unchanged.
- `fixed` waves are never passed to the sequencer (assertable via a spy/injected sequencer) and match their authored composition exactly.
- `dynamic` waves differ between at least two distinct seeds, and are identical for the same seed (test asserts both).
- `curve` and `fixed` waves are identical regardless of seed.
- Malformed/unknown mode rows and unresolvable `fixed` waves degrade safely (no crash; campaign remains playable).
- The Vite dev writer accepts valid `generation` values and rejects an invalid value with HTTP 400.
- Documentation (README, GDD, design doc and module comments) describes the three modes, the default and the seed/RNG contract for `dynamic`.
- New unit/integration tests cover the codec, mode dispatch, seed determinism and `fixed` sourcing; the full suite passes.

## Key Files

- `src/core/configTypes.ts` — add `generation` to `DifficultyCurveRow`.
- `src/core/csv.ts` — extend the difficulty-curve codec/validator.
- `vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.ts` — whitelist/validate the new column.
- `src/data/difficulty-curves.csv` — add the column to the seed config.
- `src/waves/sequencedLevels.ts` — mode dispatch, seed threading and `fixed` sourcing.
- `src/core/configStore.ts` — `defaultDifficultyCurves()` mode defaults.
- `src/scenes/PlayScene.ts` — thread the run seed into the builder for `dynamic` waves.
- `src/waves/WaveManager.ts` — verify injection seam; minimal change expected.
- Tests: `src/core/csv.test.ts`, `src/waves/sequencedLevels.test.ts`, `src/core/configStore.test.ts`.
data.title: Per-wave generation modes: curve-fixed, hand-authored fixed and dynamic runtime regeneration

## Summary
Unit tests for the `MineralHold` capacity progression logic before implementation.

## Acceptance Criteria
- **[ ] AC1 — First hold at 5** — test asserts the first hold is full at 5 minerals, not before.
- **[ ] AC2 — Doubling progression** — test asserts capacity(n) = 5 × 2^(n−1) after successive resolveHold() calls: 5 → 10 → 20 → 40.
- **[ ] AC3 — Run-scoped reset** — test asserts startGame() / re-init resets capacity to 5.
- **[ ] AC5 — Overflow preserved and clamped** — test asserts overflow carries into the next hold and the store is clamped to [0, capacity].

**Key Files:**
- `src/core/mineralHold.test.ts`
